target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is educationally valuable and worth allowing in schools
objection: AG2 argues that real-animal dissection is not educationally irreplaceable because synthetic anatomical models and computer simulations can teach the same core anatomy and still let students practice observation and interpretation without killing or dismembering animals.

target: AG1’s ethical justification that dissection is acceptable because most specimens are already dead and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts
objection: AG2 objects that “already dead” or “byproduct” status does not make dissection ethically acceptable, because dissection animals are supplied through inhumane methods and, according to the stance, about 99% are wild-caught, which harms local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that models and simulations can teach the same core concepts and skills as real dissection
objection: AG1 counters that this replacement claim is weak because real dissection provides direct tactile contact with actual tissues, exposure to natural anatomical variation, and hands-on procedural experience that models and simulations cannot fully replicate; therefore, the educational value of dissection is not fully substitutable.

target: AG1’s insistence that animal dissection is educationally irreplaceable
objection: AG2 repeats that synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same core structures and relationships while still developing observation, interpretation, and recording skills, so dissection is not uniquely necessary for learning biology.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-dead animals and byproducts removes the ethical problem
objection: AG2 reiterates that the sourcing of dissection animals is the real issue: the supply methods are reported as inhumane and the practice contributes to wild capture and biodiversity loss, so the “already dead/byproduct” rationale does not make the practice ethically acceptable.

target: AG2’s assumption that dissection demand mainly causes harm through wild capture and biodiversity loss
objection: AG1 argues that if most dissection animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts headed for landfills, then the causal link between classroom dissection demand and wild-capture/biodiversity harm does not hold, so the ethical objection is weakened.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is defensible because it uses already-dead animals and byproducts
objection: AG2 restates that the practice is still objectionable because the animal-supply chain is harmful and dissection demand contributes to wild capture; thus, the environmental and ethical tradeoffs remain unacceptable even if some specimens are already dead.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can teach the same skills as dissection
objection: AG1 argues that the claim is weak because real dissection uniquely requires students to manipulate actual tissues, make delicate cuts, and perceive real 3D anatomical relationships, which builds fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination that simulations cannot fully reproduce.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s learning benefits are irreplaceable
objection: AG2 repeats that synthetic models and simulations can teach the same anatomy, observation, interpretation, and recording skills without using dead animals, so dissection is not educationally necessary.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection does not meaningfully contribute to biodiversity harm because specimens are already dead or byproducts
objection: AG2 again objects that the broader sourcing reality matters more than the “already dead” framing: if around 99% of animals are wild-caught, dissection demand still reduces local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection demand heavily relies on wild-caught animals
objection: AG1 says that if dissection specimens are mostly already-dead animals and byproducts, then the wild-capture-based biodiversity harm story does not apply, so dissection is ethically more defensible as productive use of existing dead material.

target: AG1’s claim that harm is minimized because specimens are already dead/byproducts
objection: AG2 responds that the “already dead” framing does not eliminate the environmental harm, because the stance is that about 99% of dissection animals are still caught in the wild and that sourcing reduces local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that models and simulations can teach the same core anatomy and relationships while avoiding animal harm
objection: AG1 argues that this depends on an overly strong assumption of full educational replaceability; real dissection uniquely develops tactile discrimination, spatial understanding, and careful structural identification that models and simulations simplify away.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is educationally necessary and that ethical concerns are reduced by the use of already-dead/byproduct animals
objection: AG2 repeats that dissection is not necessary for biology learning and that the stance’s sourcing concerns remain significant because dissection animals are reported to be largely wild-caught, which harms biodiversity.

target: AG2’s premise that synthetic models and simulations can teach the same skills as dissection
objection: AG1 argues that dissection requires real-time cutting, handling of real tissue, and recognition of natural variation in three dimensions, producing fine motor and hand-eye coordination benefits that non-tactile substitutes cannot fully replicate.

target: AG1’s broader claim that dissection should be allowed because it provides irreplaceable learning and is ethically acceptable
objection: AG2 again objects that dissection is not the only way to learn anatomy or develop observation/recording skills, and that the supply-chain impacts are still significant because dissection animals are allegedly mostly wild-caught.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary because alternatives and medical training do not require it
objection: AG1 responds that even if AP/NGSS and medical schools do not require it, dissection still has educational value: it gives real-specimen experience, builds practical skills, and inspires science careers, while the ethical objection is weakened if specimens are already dead byproducts rather than freshly sourced wild animals.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is useful even though not required by AP/NGSS or medical training
objection: AG2 reasserts that dissection is unnecessary and that the harm from the supply chain remains because the stance says most dissection animals are wild-caught, so schools do not need to use real animals to meet learning goals.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can fully match dissection’s learning outcomes and that dissection is ethically unacceptable
objection: AG1 objects that models and simulations cannot fully replicate the fine motor, hand-eye, and real-specimen observational experience of dissection, and that if over 98% of specimens are already dead byproducts, the wild-capture harm mechanism the opposition cites does not fit the actual sourcing context.

target: AG1’s claim that models and simulations can’t fully replicate dissection’s learning outcomes
objection: AG2 counters that this assumes real specimens are necessary for the relevant skills, but synthetic models and simulations can be designed to train tool handling, spatial identification, and recognition of anatomical variation, so there is no educational necessity for dead real specimens.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is not irreplaceable and is ethically problematic
objection: AG1 argues again that the hands-on, real-specimen experience of dissection builds skills and motivation that models cannot fully match, and that if specimens are already dead byproducts, the claimed ethical harm from wild-capture incentives does not accurately describe the practice.

target: AG1’s assumption that the main harm problem disappears if specimens are already dead byproducts
objection: AG2 challenges that sourcing assumption directly, saying that in the relevant supply picture about 99% of dissection animals are wild-caught, so the ecological harm from wild capture remains operative.

target: AG1’s broader defense that dissection is useful despite not being required and that ethical concerns do not apply in the same way
objection: AG2 says the opposition is broader than just biodiversity loss from wild capture: the animal-supply chain is generally inhumane, and because dissection is not required by AP/NGSS or medical training, schools need not accept those harms.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is broadly ethically unacceptable because of supply-chain harms
objection: AG1 argues that if classrooms predominantly use already-dead animals and meat-industry byproducts, then dissection does not create an additional ongoing wild-capture harm stream; instead, it is a productive use of animals that would otherwise be discarded.

target: AG1’s claim that the byproduct/already-dead framing removes the ethical and environmental objection
objection: AG2 responds that the framing does not remove the harm because dissection demand can still depend heavily on wild-caught animals, so the ecological incentive and biodiversity loss remain in the overall procurement system.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection demand still creates harmful incentives even when specimens are byproducts
objection: AG1 reiterates that if over 98% of specimens are already dead and fetal pigs are byproducts destined for landfill, then school dissection is largely using existing waste material rather than driving new wild-capture harm, so the ethical/environmental objection is not intact.

target: AG1’s assumption that byproduct sourcing means schools are not meaningfully driving wild capture
objection: AG2 counters that the supply chain is not reliably satisfied by byproducts alone; dissection programs still obtain many animals through wild capture, so dissection demand can continue to incentivize ecological harm.

target: AG2’s claim that the wild-capture harm mechanism remains central despite byproduct sourcing
objection: AG1 says that in ordinary school dissection the specimens are overwhelmingly already deceased and sourced from byproduct channels, so the specific mechanism of ongoing wild-capture causing biodiversity loss does not apply in the way the opposition claims.

target: AG1’s claim that “already dead” or “byproduct” sourcing removes the upstream harm
objection: AG2 objects that byproducts are not harm-free: they exist because animals were acquired and killed upstream, and if the supply chain involves wildlife harvesting or capture, then dissection demand still creates incentives that can reduce local populations and biodiversity.
